episode.throughLine: A boy who found public speaking painful used writing and quiet, then recited a poem of his own and found a way to work with speech.

contentProfile.contentNote: Childhood stuttering and ridicule, with respected silence and written communication; no diagnosis or cure narrative.

facts.statement: Jones recalled that from about age ten a teacher accepted written reports and written examinations instead of spoken answers.

sourceRefs.locator: 1996 interview answer beginning 'I'm still a stutterer', through 'I became a writer'

facts.statement: As a child Jones found speaking embarrassing and difficult; he recalled other children laughing at his attempts to read verses in Sunday school.

sourceRefs.locator: June 3, 2005 Paula Zahn interview, question 'Why did you spend so much time in silence as a kid?' and next answer

facts.statement: Jones said he wanted to stop attending church and Sunday school because of stuttering and children's laughter, and his family accepted his decision.

sourceRefs.locator: 1993 Terry Gross interview, rebroadcast August 23, 2002, question about adults coaxing him to talk

facts.statement: Jones recalled communicating his needs to his family, calling farm animals, and talking to his dog, but not wanting to speak to strangers at the house.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening Jones answer: 'I did the basics' through 'I hid in the state of muteness'

facts.statement: Jones remembered enjoying quiet when people respected him, left him alone and did not probe him.

sourceRefs.locator: 1996 answer beginning 'Oral examinations?' and following sentence beginning 'As long as people respected'

facts.statement: Jones recalled writing poetry privately in high school; Donald Crouch discovered it and encouraged him to speak the words aloud.

sourceRefs.locator: Finding My Voice, paragraphs beginning 'Professor Crouch discovered' and 'The poem was called'

facts.statement: Crouch read a poem and challenged Jones to prove he had written it by reciting it to the class from memory.

sourceRefs.locator: Finding My Voice, paragraph beginning 'Professor Crouch discovered'

facts.statement: Jones recalled the allegation of copying as a shock; he recognized the poem's resemblance to Longfellow but said he had not stolen it.

sourceRefs.locator: Answer describing Crouch, beginning 'He one day discovered that I wrote poetry' through 'not certainly stolen'

facts.statement: Jones said he accepted the challenge and recited the poem because he wanted to prove he was not a plagiarist.

sourceRefs.locator: Finding My Voice, paragraph beginning 'Professor Crouch discovered', final two sentences

facts.statement: Jones recalled standing up, reciting his poem and not stuttering.

sourceRefs.locator: 1996 question 'What was the poem he finally got you to read aloud?' and answer ending 'Nice surprise'

facts.statement: Asked what he felt at the recital, Jones declined to call it happy or pleasurable; he described shock and feeling in trouble.

sourceRefs.locator: 1996 question 'What came over you at that moment?' and complete answer

facts.statement: Jones said that reading his poems aloud helped him speak and deal with his stutter; he did not know whether Crouch's challenge was a trick.

sourceRefs.locator: Finding My Voice, paragraph beginning 'The poem was called', final three sentences

facts.statement: Jones described his period of rarely speaking as lasting until fourteen, without giving the recital an exact calendar date. The Fresh Air program introduction describes the period of minimal speech as ages six to fourteen; individual Sunday-school events are undated.

sourceRefs.locator: Finding My Voice, opening sentence and high-school poem account
Jones segment introduction ending 'ages of 6 and 14 when he barely spoke at all'

facts.statement: In a 2014 interview Jones rejected the claim that he had overcome stuttering and described working with and around it.

sourceRefs.locator: Mitch Mattson interview, question about overcoming childhood stutter, first three sentences of Jones's answer

facts.statement: James Earl Jones was an actor whose film voice roles include Darth Vader in Star Wars.

sourceRefs.locator: James Earl Jones, 2011 Governors Awards tribute, screen career and voice-role paragraphs

arc.canonicalText: At school, he answered with a pencil. He was about ten. That is how he remembered beginning more demanding schoolwork. He had things to report, things he knew, and a teacher who accepted written answers. Even examinations that called for speaking could be done in writing. The teacher did not require him to say the answers aloud. He could put them on paper.
arc.sourceNote: CRAFT HOLD: the source describes a repeated school arrangement from about ten, not one located examination. This draft does not invent a date, room layout, or teacher's gesture. The wider 6-14 episode range accommodates undated Sunday-school memories.

arc.canonicalText: Reading aloud in the children's religious class brought laughter. He tried to read the verses, and other children laughed at his speech. For him, stuttering was embarrassing and painful. The laughter hurt. He could be among other children, with the same task before them, and still struggle to speak. The children laughed.
arc.sourceNote: CRAFT HOLD: Jones describes recurring Sunday-school readings, not a verified single occasion. Exact age and sequence relative to the school-writing arrangement are not established. No assertion that every quiet period was distress.

arc.canonicalText: He wanted to stop going to the religious classes. His family accepted that. He no longer had to keep attending the place where the children laughed at his stutter. At home, he still let his family know what he needed. On the farm, he called to the animals while doing his chores. He talked to the dog. The dog was his friend and did not challenge him. But when strangers came to the house, he did not want to speak to them. He was not ready for that encounter.
arc.sourceNote: CRAFT HOLD: the small documented response is withdrawal from Sunday school, followed by a truthful summary of communication at home. The record does not locate a single request/conversation or date; do not invent one. No claim that withdrawal caused the poetry turn.

arc.canonicalText: He could enjoy being quiet when people respected it. He liked being left alone without questions pressing him to speak. He also wrote. By high school he was making poems of his own, privately. His English teacher discovered them. The teacher encouraged him to give the written words a voice. Then he read a poem and challenged the boy's claim to have written it. He wanted the boy to recite it from memory before the class. The suggestion that he had copied it shocked him. He recognized another poet's rhythm in his writing, but he had not stolen the poem. The poem was his.
arc.sourceNote: Honest compression into high school. CRAFT HOLD: no sustained documented failed effort between writing and recitation; the challenge supplies pressure but not the recipe's full struggle. The teacher's intent is expressly unknown.

arc.canonicalText: He stood up in front of the class and recited the poem. He wanted to show that he had written it himself. He spoke from memory. This time he did not stutter. The words reached the class in his own voice. He had answered the teacher's challenge. In his memory, the surprise was not something he could simply call happiness. He felt shocked and in trouble. He did not put a label of pleasure on it. He had spoken.
arc.sourceNote: Located classroom recital, probable retrospective evidence. The exact date is not supplied; age around fourteen follows the memoir's endpoint. No invented applause, smiling classmates, teacher satisfaction, instant confidence, or known trick.

arc.canonicalText: Reading his poems aloud gave him a way to work with speech. He could take words he had written and say them. The teacher had encouraged that connection between the page and the voice. He kept reading his poems aloud, and found that it helped. He did not know whether the challenge had been a trick. That question stayed unanswered. The boy who had been allowed to answer examinations in writing was speaking his own poems. He still had the page.
arc.sourceNote: Stops at poetry and resumed speech. CRAFT HOLD: available post-recital evidence is a summary, not a dated routine. Later first-person statement j14 stays in the fold and prevents a cure reading; no lifetime career list or post-1945 episode is added.

arc.canonicalText:
His name was James Earl Jones.

He was an actor who gave Darth Vader his voice in the Star Wars films. Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you. You do not have to make every part of yourself easy for other people. You are allowed to be quiet.
arc.sourceNote: Name and familiar work appear only here; permission does not require speaking, overcoming disability, or performing.

dramatizationLimits: No invented episode, audience reaction, emotion, room detail, medical explanation, or dialogue.
All childhood recollections remain probable; the brief memory cues identify the nature of the telling.
Quiet and writing are forms of communication, not failures requiring a triumphant speaking outcome.
avoidRules: Do not claim he stopped all speech or spoke only to animals.
Do not claim the poem cured stuttering or that the recital felt uncomplicatedly happy.
Do not say Crouch knowingly pretended to doubt authorship; Jones said he did not know.
Keep exact age uncertainty and scene/response/struggle gaps explicit until reviewed.
